newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania revolt spreads as rebels shun peace moves.
newsitem.headline: Albania revolt spreads as rebels shun peace moves.

text.p: Albania's revolt spread through most of the south of the country on Monday as the army pulled back in disarray and rebels ignored a political deal thrashed out by President Sali Berisha and the opposition.

Latest areas to fall were the ancient town of Berat, abandoned without a fight by the army, and the nearby town of Kucove, where residents pillaged an air force base, one of two important military airfields in Albania. One person died after being hit by a stray bullet from celebratory fire.
Reports reaching Tirana indicated the towns of Polican and Corovode, south of the capital, were also in rebel hands.

Underlining the growing instability of the situation in southern Albania, a series of explosions rocked a rebel-held arms depot in the village of Lazarat, sending residents fleeing from the area around the barracks and arsenal.

A journalist working for Radio France Internationale was fired on in his car near the town of Fier, but only grazed. It was believed to be the first time a reporter covering the unrest had been shot at.
Rebels had to fight for Permet, a remote mountain locality where five people were killed and six were injured.

The townspeople began burying their dead on Monday, in a funeral that swelled into a protest rally with about 3,000 people shouting "Down with Berisha, down with the murderer" as youths fired their looted Kalashnikov rifles into the air.
Rebels on the streets said they supported the idea of an all-party government under Berisha's weekend deal, but refused to down their weapons until Berisha resigned.
They accused him of allowing pyramid schemes to flourish before collapsing with the savings of hundreds of thousands.
"We don't trust him any more," said Sokol, one of the Berat rebels. "He deserves to be hanged by his tongue."
In Tirana, the head of one of the largest investment groups, Vehbi Alimucaj, announced on television that all his investors would be reimbursed in two months.

In Rome, the Foreign Ministry said Italy's ambassador to Tirana was holding talks with rebel leaders from southern Albania on an Italian naval vessel in the Adriatic to foster a dialogue between them and the authorities.
Berisha met leaders of his own Democratic Party and the opposition in Tirana to form an interim government due to oversee early general elections due by June under the accord.

Perikli Teta, a leader of the opposition Democratic Alliance, told Reuters the two sides had agreed to split ministries equally between government and opposition parties. Under the deal, the prime minister would be appointed by Berisha and the deputy prime minister by the opposition.
Tough discussions were expected on security portfolios, particulary the interior ministry. Parliament was in session to approve an amnesty to rebels who hand in weapons within a week.

More than 40 people have died in the violence in the past week. Before the weekend deal, parliament had imposed a state of emergency and then re-elected Berisha to a second five-year term, enraging the opposition and dismaying foreign countries.
Sunday's accord followed Berisha's reversal of his refusal to form a coalition with the Socialists, heirs to Albania's Communist party that ran a repressive regime for 45 years.
The rebel spokesman in Berat said the army moved out of its barracks on Sunday soon after state television broadcast parts of the meeting showing the accord being clinched.
Shots reverberated throughout the town and surrounding hills and most residents appeared to have remained indoors to avoid the risk of being hit by stray bullets.
Roadblocks were absent on the main highway south of the Shkumbini River that divides the Balkan country into northern and southern halves.
The only army tanks visible were clustered in a group just south of the river apparently guarding the road north to Tirana and east to government held-towns like Elbasan.
